title: megalithic tombs persisted into the bronze age in spain
dek: new research shows collective tombs at Trafalgar were built and used during the early 2nd millennium BC
body: archaeologists working on the southern coast of spain have uncovered two monumental tombs that challenge how we think about the bronze age. the Trafalgar necropolis near the Strait of Gibraltar contains remains of multiple individuals buried in large collective structures once thought to belong to an earlier copper age. radiocarbon dates place the activity of both tombs between roughly 1875 and 1625 BC.

the discovery comes from a study published in PLOS One that examined 16 individuals recovered from the two tombs. researchers from the University of Cádiz and collaborating institutions obtained these dates directly from the human remains. the findings place Trafalgar among the latest known examples of megalithic collective burial traditions on the Iberian Peninsula, a region where such large communal tombs were increasingly being replaced by smaller, individual burials during the same period.

what makes Trafalgar unusual is the absence of earlier occupation beneath the monuments. at many other sites, bronze age burials inside megaliths represent centuries‑long reuse of structures built during the copper age. at Trafalgar, however, the team has found no evidence for earlier burials or activity. this suggests the tombs may have been constructed only shortly before the dated interments, rather than being ancient monuments put back into use.

the landscape around Trafalgar is defined by the sea. the necropolis sits on the southern coast, a location that may have influenced why communities chose this spot for new monumental construction during a time when such traditions were fading elsewhere. the two tombs maintained a collective funerary practice with much deeper roots in Iberian prehistory, even as funerary customs were shifting across much of the peninsula.

if future research confirms that the Trafalgar tombs were built in the early 2nd millennium BC, it would show that monumental collective tomb building survived in southern Iberia much later than previously thought. instead of simply recycling monuments left behind by copper age communities, bronze age populations were still creating new megalithic burial landscapes of their own. the site’s potential extent remains unknown, as strong winds and shifting sands in the coastal zone constantly re‑bury exposed remains.

the absence of earlier archaeological material around the necropolis supports the possibility that the burial landscape was created during the bronze age rather than inherited from a much earlier community. more monuments could be waiting to be found around Trafalgar, and they may help us understand how long megalithic burial traditions survived in southern Iberia. conservation work and further excavation will be needed to determine the full scope of the site.

doesnt_show: whether the tombs were originally constructed in the early 2nd millennium BC or whether they represent a brief, localized tradition that did not spread widely. the exact construction date of the monuments remains uncertain.
settle: precise radiocarbon dating of the tombs' original construction phases, ideally from undisturbed primary fills or associated architectural features.
